gist: A narrated case study of how Exxon (formerly Standard Oil of New Jersey), convinced by a 1960 internal report that oil was no longer a growth business, spent two decades diversifying into chemicals, venture investments and finally office equipment — rolling Vydec, Qyx, QWIP and 12 other holdings into Exxon Information Systems in 1978 to attack IBM and Xerox, and liquidating it by 1984. It doubles as a corporate-venture post-mortem on Zilog, which Exxon solely funded in 1975 and whose Z80 lost the IBM PC socket partly because Exxon had become IBM's competitor; the failure hardened Exxon into a pure oil-and-gas capital allocator under Lee Raymond.

themes.theme: The 1960 'oil is not a growth business' verdict

insights.claim: Standard Oil of New Jersey's 1960 Jones Report concluded that the oil glut would persist and that oil and gas was no longer a growth business — not that the company should leave oil, but that future oil investments would deliver ever-worsening returns, so new revenue lines were needed to make it a growth stock again.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: The canonical template for commodity-major diversification: a mature-returns diagnosis, correct on the macro, still produced twenty years of value-destroying capital allocation — worth applying to any incumbent today justifying adjacency M&A with 'our core is ex-growth'.

insights.claim: In 1958 Jersey Standard sold more oil than ever yet earned only about a third of the profits it made at the start of the decade, as the Iranian consortium settlement plus rising Soviet Volga-Urals output deepened a glut that held posted prices at roughly $2-3 per barrel until 1970.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Record volumes with collapsing profit is the classic signature of new marginal supply entering a market; the 12-year price stagnation that followed shows how long a supply-driven glut can suppress commodity earnings.

insights.claim: Jersey Standard lifted Esso Chemical's annual investment budget from an average of $53 million in 1961-1963 to $257 million in 1964 and by 1965 the unit returned just 4% on net total assets, with thermoplastics and fertilizers oversupplied and losing millions.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: A near-5x capex step-up producing a 4% asset return within two years is a reusable warning sign: speed of deployment, not the thesis, is what destroys returns in capital-intensive expansions.

insights.claim: Jersey Standard CEO Jack Rathbone publicly identified petrochemicals as a fashionable, crowded entry that would lose money for many entrants — while his own company was simultaneously making exactly that mistake against incumbents like Phillips, Royal Dutch Shell, Standard of Indiana and Standard of California.
insights.speaker: Monroe 'Jack' Rathbone, Jersey Standard CEO (quoted by narrator)
insights.so_what: Management correctly diagnosing a crowded trade is no protection against entering it; treat peer-wide simultaneous entry into an adjacency as a margin-compression signal regardless of what the CEO says about discipline.
insights.quote: this dashing into chemicals is going to lose a lot of money for some companies, because petrochemicals are not a guaranteed gold mine ... And it won't be us.

insights.claim: Esso Chemical only became a durable earner in the 1970s after management curtailed the foreign build-out and refocused on specialty chemicals that produced weaker top-line numbers but hundreds of millions of dollars of profit by the end of the decade.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: The recovery path from a commodity-chemicals blowup is narrowing to specialty niches and accepting lower revenue — a pattern still relevant when judging chemical-segment restructurings.

themes.theme: Jersey/Exxon Enterprises as a venture portfolio

insights.claim: Jersey Enterprises, founded in 1963, screened ten broad categories each judged capable of birthing a new $100 million company, and nearly all failed — American Cryogenics (bought for $37 million in January 1964, dropped in 1968), a Nestlé-affiliate hydrocarbon-grown bacterial protein called WO-100, petroleum-residue building blocks, medical instruments, nuclear energy and fuel cells — leaving information technology as one of the few survivors.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Corporate venture arms show venture-like failure rates but without venture-like winners, because the parent keeps funding and steering losers instead of cutting them fast.

insights.claim: Vydec's estimated $24 million of 1977 revenue was immaterial next to the $48.6 billion Exxon took in from oil that year, which is the structural reason no venture inside the portfolio could ever matter to the parent.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Apply the same denominator test to any megacap's 'new growth vertical': if a successful outcome is sub-1% of revenue, the option value is in the narrative, not the numbers.

insights.claim: Exxon managers admitted in 1976 there was no grand scheme or master plan behind the portfolio, which by then also held Periphonics (a computer that imitated human voices) and Micro-Bit (electron beam accessed memory) alongside word processors.
insights.speaker: Exxon managers (reported by narrator)
insights.so_what: An acquisition set with no articulable synthesis thesis is a red flag that later gets retrofitted with a strategy — as Exxon did in 1978 when it declared war on IBM.

themes.theme: Zilog: the double edge of strategic capital

insights.claim: Exxon Enterprises became Zilog's sole investor in 1975 because the post-bubble venture market had collapsed — Federico Faggin recalled only about $10 million of technology investments being made in all of 1975 — and Faggin has acknowledged Zilog would probably never have gotten off the ground without Exxon.
insights.speaker: Federico Faggin, Zilog cofounder (via Computer History Museum oral history, relayed by narrator)
insights.so_what: Capital droughts hand pricing power and access to top founding teams to whoever is still writing checks — the entry point that later produced Zilog's fab and the Z80.

insights.claim: In Zilog's early days the Exxon affiliation was itself a sales asset that won design wins, with cofounder Ralph Ungermann pitching customers on the combination of Exxon's balance sheet and Intel-trained engineering talent.
insights.speaker: Ralph Ungermann, Zilog cofounder (relayed by narrator)
insights.so_what: For components sold to enterprises, perceived supplier solvency is part of the product — a corporate backer can shorten the sales cycle before it becomes a liability.
insights.quote: the money of Exxon and the brains of Intel

insights.claim: Former Zilog employee Bernard Pueto attributed the company's drift to Exxon giving it too much money and too many directions, pushing it into projects it should not have pursued while inexperienced young managers failed to push back, and Faggin ended up spending more time in New York managing Exxon than in California with customers.
insights.speaker: Bernard Pueto, former Zilog employee (relayed by narrator)
insights.so_what: Oversupply of capital plus parent-directed scope creep is a distinct failure mode from underfunding, and it also fractured the founding team — Ungermann left over the Exxon disagreements.
insights.quote: gave them too much money and too many directions

insights.claim: Exxon's decision to compete with IBM cost its own portfolio company the biggest design win of the era: Faggin later confirmed that Exxon's status as an IBM competitor was one reason IBM chose Intel's 8088 over the Zilog Z80 for the IBM PC.
insights.speaker: Federico Faggin (relayed by narrator)
insights.so_what: The clearest lesson for founders and investors weighing strategic money: a corporate parent's conflicts propagate down to the startup's customer list, and one lost socket can decide an industry's standard.

themes.theme: Exxon Information Systems declares war on IBM

insights.claim: In late 1978 Exxon merged Vydec, the QWIP fax machine and the Z80-powered $1,390 Qyx 'intelligent' typewriter with 12 other prior investments into Exxon Information Systems, which did roughly $100 million of revenue in 1978 and $200 million in 1979, with the stated goal of becoming a major office-equipment player within three to five years.
insights.speaker: Ben Sykes, head of Jersey/Exxon Enterprises (figures relayed by narrator)
insights.so_what: The revenue base was doubling when the roll-up was announced, which is precisely when such programs attract the most capital and the least scrutiny.

insights.claim: The 1980 bull case, voiced by a Yankee Group analyst, was that Exxon's office-systems business would rival or surpass its oil business, underpinned by a forecast $150-200 billion IT market by the end of the 1980s and a 10% Exxon share — a projection that the subsequent 1984 shutdown falsified entirely.
insights.speaker: Yankee Group analyst (quoted by narrator)
insights.so_what: A cautionary datapoint on sell-side TAM-times-assumed-share math: the market forecast was roughly right while the share assumption was worthless, which is the usual way such targets fail.
insights.quote: It seems likely that the [office system] business they are building now will rival, if not surpass, their oil business ultimately

insights.claim: Skeptics answered with arithmetic rather than technology: Exxon booked $84 billion of revenue in 1979 on second-energy-crisis prices, so even an outcome as spectacular as matching Xerox would have added only about $7 billion.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator), summarizing contemporary skeptics
insights.so_what: Sizing the best realistic case against the existing revenue base is the fastest way to kill a diversification narrative before assessing its execution risk.
insights.quote: For Exxon, that's a drop of oil into the barrel.

insights.claim: Exxon Information Systems began life as a 6,000-employee roll-up of small unrelated companies with a 40-page organization chart, and Wang Labs EVP John Cunningham publicly doubted anyone could integrate them.
insights.speaker: John Cunningham, EVP at Wang Labs (quoted by narrator)
insights.so_what: Integration cost scales with the number of unrelated acquired units, not their combined revenue — a useful prior when a conglomerate announces a 'consolidated' new division.
insights.quote: If God himself came down in a junior businessman's uniform, worked very hard for three years, and got very lucky, he'd still have a tough time pulling those companies together

insights.claim: Exxon assembled a portfolio of dedicated word processors and standalone office machines on the eve of the PC revolution — the Apple II arrived in April 1977 and paired with VisiCalc, and the Z80-powered TRS-80 ate into the same market — so the 1981 IBM PC obsoleted a lineup Exxon had spent a decade acquiring.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Slow corporate acquisition cycles are structurally dangerous in technology because the category can be redefined between thesis and integration — Exxon's own chip powered the machines displacing its products.

insights.claim: Product execution failed on every front: the second-generation QWIP took six years to develop and shipped with a jamming paper feeder, Vydec was locked out of US government work over security issues, a Qyx typewriter caught fire inside Exxon's own New York headquarters, and Exxon's Houston marketing division — which preferred Wang — was forced to take Exxon machines and returned them a year later.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Six-year development cycles in a market turning over in three, plus a captive internal customer handing the product back, are as clean a read on uncompetitiveness as a business can produce.

insights.claim: Faggin described an Exxon decision process in which every level deferred upward until Ben Sykes, the senior man, said yes or no — an escalation culture incompatible with a fast-moving, talent-centric industry.
insights.speaker: Federico Faggin (quoted by narrator)
insights.so_what: Decision latency, not capital or technology, is the binding constraint when a capital-project organization tries to run a product business.
insights.quote: the lower guy on the totem pole would look up, the other guy would look up at the next, and Ben Sykes who was the senior guy would say, “Yes,” or “No.”

insights.claim: Exxon cut Exxon Information Systems twice in 1981 from 6,000 to 4,000 employees, staggered on two more years with annual reports citing narrowing losses and new products, and only admitted failure in 1984 — after which leftover obsolete QWIP machines were bulldozed at a dump.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: The three-year gap between the market's verdict and management's admission, narrated through 'losses narrowing' disclosure language, is the standard timeline for a large-cap to exit a failed venture.

themes.theme: Exit economics and the Raymond doctrine

insights.claim: Zilog, the last Exxon Enterprises holding to go, was sold in the late 1980s via a Warburg Pincus-backed management buyout at roughly 4 times free cash flow, taken public in 1991 and acquired in 1997 for $527 million, returning Warburg about 12 times on a $17 million investment.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: Orphaned technology assets inside a retreating conglomerate are the cheapest entry points in the market — 4x free cash flow for a franchise chip business — and the buyer, not the corporate parent, captures the value.

insights.claim: The Exxon Information Systems failure imprinted itself on senior management and was institutionalized when Lee Raymond became CEO in 1993 and spent two decades redoubling on oil and gas, by which point ExxonMobil had become the biggest and most profitable company the world had then seen.
insights.speaker: Jon Y (narrator)
insights.so_what: A failed diversification can be worth more than a successful one if it produces lasting capital-allocation discipline — the direct lineage from the 1984 shutdown to ExxonMobil's peak-profitability era.
insights.quote: They were oil men. Nothing more.
